title: The Kon-Tiki Raft Voyage
text:
The Norwegian Thor Heyerdahl believed that people from South America could have reached Polynesia in prehistoric times on balsa rafts. Experts told him such a raft would sink or fall apart. In 1947 he decided to prove it could be done.

He and five companions, four Norwegians and one Swede, built a raft of nine balsa logs lashed together with hemp rope, copying early Spanish descriptions of Peruvian rafts, with a small bamboo cabin and a square sail. They left Callao, Peru, on 28 April 1947. Each man had a role. Herman Watzinger, an engineer, took weather and current measurements. Knut Haugland and Torstein Raaby, radio operators who had served in the wartime resistance, kept contact with amateur radio stations. Erik Hesselberg navigated. Bengt Danielsson, the Swede, looked after the stores. Everyone took turns at the steering oar and on watch.

Heyerdahl's book describes the six men living for over three months on a deck the size of a small room, eating flying fish that landed on board at night, joking, and keeping strict watches. When Watzinger fell overboard and the raft could not turn back, Haugland jumped in with a line and the others hauled both men back.

After 101 days and some 4,300 miles (about 6,900 km), the raft was driven onto the reef of Raroia in the Tuamotu Islands on 7 August. All six men survived and waded ashore.
lesson: Small crews in close quarters hold together through clear roles, shared routines and humor. Make sure everyone knows their job and trusts the others to do theirs.
people: Thor Heyerdahl, Herman Watzinger, Erik Hesselberg, Knut Haugland, Torstein Raaby, Bengt Danielsson
location: Pacific Ocean, from Callao, Peru, to Raroia, French Polynesia
caveat: The voyage proved the crossing was possible, but most scholars reject Heyerdahl's theory that Polynesia was settled mainly from South America.
